title: Thymosin β4-sulfoxide attenuates inflammatory cell infiltration and promotes cardiac wound healing

what_it_measured.text: To determine a potential mechanism, we investigated whether Tβ4-SO, in the presence of IFN-γ, might act to increase intracellular ROS and thus provoke oxidative stress-induced apoptosis20.
Extrapolating the animal model findings to human monocytes/macrophages we investigated the response to inflammatory stimuli in the presence of Tβ4-SO.

dose.text: Where indicated, cells were also treated with Tβ4 (100ng/ml), Tβ4-SO (100ng/ml) or PBS.
Nonadherent (non-macrophage) cells were removed from the well with vigorous washing and macrophages were stimulated with IFN-γ (50ng/ml), PBS supplemented with 100ng/ml Tβ4SO or PBS alone.

route.text: On recovery, animals received interperitoneal (i.p.) injection of either Tβ4 (6mgkg−1), Tβ4-SO (6mgkg−1) or vehicle (PBS).

endpoint.text: We next assessed whether effects on CD14+ cell adhesion/dispersal might be accompanied by elevated cell death and observed Tβ4-SO significantly increased the number of trypan blue positive cells compared to IFN-γ and control treated cultures (Tβ4SO: 135833 +/− 22928 SEM versus IFN-γ: 55833 +/− 2203 SEM versus co: 33333 +/− 833 SEM; n=3; p≤0.05; Fig 5d).
Scanning densitometry was performed and signal quantified using ImageJ.
Infarct size was assessed using late gadolinium enhancement (LGE): 0.6mmolkg−1 Gd-DTPA was Nat Commun.

reported_results.text: Levels of Tβ4-SO increased rapidly, one hour post-wounding, by approximately 5-fold from 2.0% +/− 1.4% SEM to 10.4% +/− 1.96% SEM (n=100 wounded tail fins/treatment, n=3 experimental replicates; Student’s ttest, p ≤ 0.01; Fig. 1c).
Tβ4 treatment attenuated this increase with fewer MPO+ cells present (co: 70 + 14.5 S.E.M versus Tβ4: 30 + 19.1 SEM, p≤ 0.15) at the site of injury at both stages (Fig. 3a-d).

Increase in infarct volume (late gadolinium enhancement; LGE) was significantly higher in PBS compared to Tβ4-treated mice; persisting up to day 28 post-MI (co: 43.3 ± 4.9μl; n=5 versus Tβ4: 22.0 ± 5.3μl; n=4; Student’s t-test; p≤0.05; Fig. 4d) and % infarct relative to left ventricular mass (LVM) followed the same trend (day 28 post-MI: co: 27 ± 2%; n=5 versus Tβ4: 18 ± 4%; n=4; Student’s t-test, p≤0.05; Fig. 4d) indicating that Tβ4/Tβ4-SO reduced infarct size and scarring.

Tβ4-SO was significantly increased in hearts following the addition of Tβ4 across the time course of the study: percentage oxidised Tβ4 increased from 4.7 +/− 1.3% in sham control hearts to 66 +/− 5.1% at day 2 post-MI, maintained at an equivalent elevated level (68.6 +/− 9.3%) through to 28 days post-MI (n=4; repeated measures one-way ANOVA; p≤0.001).

Conversely, 4 days post-injury the total number of monocytes was significantly reduced compared to controls (co: 5.9% +/− 0.95% SEM versus Tβ4-SO: 2.7% +/− 0.4% SEM; n=4; Student’s t-test, p≤0.05; Fig. 4c).

We next investigated the anti-inflammatory activity of Tβ4-SO by flow cytometry of infarct cell suspensions and observed an early (day 2) significant increase in F4/80+ cells (co: 23.0% +/− 2.85% SEM versus Tβ4-SO: 32.0% +/− 2% SEM; n=4; Student’s t-test, p≤0.05; Fig 4a), which represented an increase in the proportion of macrophages, since the total number of monocyte (CD11bhi, [Ly6G, B220, CD49b, CD90.2, NK1.1]Low) cells remained unaltered (Fig. 4b).
